title: AI‐Driven Intelligent ECM‐Mimetic Hydrogel Scaffolds for Brain Organoid Engineering
content:
ABSTRACT
Brain organoids are increasingly used for scalable modeling of human neurodevelopment and disease, but their reproducibility and translational value remain limited by reliance on ill‐defined matrices such as Matrigel. Although Matrigel provides several brain‐relevant features, including soft, viscoelastic, and non‐fibrillar properties, its composition is poorly defined, batch‐variable, and difficult to tune in a standardized manner. Considering the physicochemical characteristics of the native brain extracellular matrix (ECM), brain organoid culture requires ECM‐like materials that reproduce brain‐specific mechanical, transport, and signaling cues rather than merely providing 3D support. This review presents a rational framework for engineering intelligent ECM‐mimetic hydrogel scaffolds for advanced brain organoid culture. It summarizes key features of the native brain ECM and introduces material rationality as the systematic selection and engineering of hydrogels according to brain‐specific biological, physical, and translational design requirements. The review also highlights how artificial intelligence (AI) can navigate high‐dimensional material design spaces through surrogate modeling, digital twins, and closed‐loop optimization informed by multi‐physics and multi‐omics feedback. Ultimately, AI‐driven scaffold design may enable more reproducible, mature, and scalable brain organoid models.

title: Temporal Fidelity Reveals Transient Dissolution Chemistry at Dynamic Electrocatalyst Interfaces
content:
Transient dissolution can be more reliably interpreted when metal release remains temporally linked to the evolving electrochemical state. By suppressing transport‐induced signal convolution, thin‐layer electrochemical inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (EC‐ICP‐MS) restores this link, resolves overlapping dissolution events, and reveals weak redox‐ and reaction‐coupled interfacial chemistry.








ABSTRACT
Dynamic electrocatalyst dissolution consists of short‐lived, potential‐dependent interfacial events tied to surface redox, reconstruction, and catalysis. Accurate interpretation of these processes requires preserving the temporal link between metal release and electrochemical state, but this link is often lost in electrochemical inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (EC‐ICP‐MS) due to transport‐induced signal convolution. Here we reduce this distortion by using thin‐layer hydrodynamic confinement to improve near‐electrode convective removal. Paired‐pulse dissolution experiments show that two consecutive 2 s dissolution inputs separated by 50 ms remain distinguishable. Cu‐pulse residence‐time‐distribution measurements and computational fluid dynamics further identify electrode‐region convective coverage and near‐electrode flow velocity as key determinants of signal broadening. Applying this temporal fidelity to representative noble‐metal, carbide, nitride, hydroxide, oxide, and single‐atom interfaces under fast cyclic voltammetry reveals distinct dynamic dissolution fingerprints. This approach further resolves weak reoxidation‐associated Ir dissolution from reduced IrOx and oxygen‐reduction‐associated suppression of spontaneous Cu release from Cu–N–C. These results highlight the importance of temporal fidelity for assigning transient dissolution chemistry at dynamic electrocatalyst interfaces.

title: Conformational Locking in Covalent Organic Frameworks Promotes Coupled H2O2 Photosynthesis and Organic Valorization
content:
Conformational locking enhances framework planarity and prolongs the charge‐separated‐state lifetime in covalent organic frameworks, promoting photocatalytic H2O2 production coupled with selective benzylamine oxidation.








ABSTRACT
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) offer a compelling platform for coupling photocatalytic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) production with organic valorization. However, the practical efficiency remains limited by rapid electron‐hole recombination. Inspired by the conformational rigidity and planar geometry imposed by peptide bonds, we develop a conformational locking strategy that introduces a fused‐ring linker, which restricts backbone rotation and thereby enhances framework planarity and conjugation, affording a series of COFs (TFPPy‐DATMBP, TFPPy‐DABP, and TFPPy‐DAPy) with progressively improved planarity and conjugation. The conformationally locked TFPPy‐DAPy achieves an impressive H2O2 production rate of 119.8 mmol g−1 h−1, with an apparent quantum yield up to 29.14% at 410 nm, while delivering a yield of >98% toward the high‐value imine product. Transient absorption spectroscopy reveals that the conformationally locked TFPPy‐DAPy extends the lifetime of the long‐lived charge‐separated state by approximately 10‐fold to 102.87 ps, compared with 10.34 ps for TFPPy‐DATMBP. This work establishes TFPPy‐DAPy as an efficient photocatalyst for fine chemical co‐production, and provides a generalizable molecular‐level design strategy for developing advanced catalysts across diverse photocatalytic applications.

title: Band‐Filling Engineering in Covalent Organic Frameworks Through Host–Guest Charge‐Transfer Interactions
content:
Introduction of controlled amounts of the electron acceptor, 7,7,8,8‐tetracyanoquinodimethane (TCNQ), into the one‐dimensional channels of tetrathiafulvalene‐containing covalent organic framework (TTF‐COF) enabled rational control over the charge states of the TTF moieties while preserving the framework structure. This band‐filling control approach, with the aid of spectroscopic measurements and theoretical calculations, enabled the emergence of Pauli‐like paramagnetism in the TCNQ‐introduced TTF‐COF hybrids.








ABSTRACT
Band‐filling engineering is one of the most rational approaches to controlling the electronic properties of inorganic solids such as cuprates, in which electron/hole doping using heterovalent substitution leads to a rigid‐band shift of the Fermi level. In organic solids, a significant obstacle to accurately predicting electronic properties is the difficulty in maintaining the packing structure during molecular substitution. Here, we utilized a covalent organic framework (COF) in which π‐conjugated electron‐donating molecules are covalently linked to form one‐dimensional pore channels. The introduction of a well‐defined amount of electron‐accepting molecules without disrupting the framework structure enabled the first successful demonstration of the deliberate band‐filling control while elucidating the charge state through various spectroscopic measurements. Enhanced electronic itinerancy facilitated by host–guest charge transfer was evidenced by spectroscopic, transport, and magnetic measurements in support of theoretical calculations. The present study opens a new avenue for exploring more advanced electronic organic solids based on band‐filling engineering.

title: Enantioselective Enyne Cyclization to Thermodynamically Favored Endocyclic Alkenes via a Rhodium‐Migration Relay
content:
A Rh‐catalyzed enantioselective arylative cyclization of 1,n‐enynes directly furnishes thermodynamically favored endocyclic alkenes bearing exocyclic stereogenic centers. A sequential 1,2‐/1,3‐/1,4‐rhodium migration relay enables C═C bond transposition and stereospecific chirality transfer beyond conventional ring closure.








ABSTRACT
Transition‐metal‐catalyzed addition/cyclizations of electrophile‐tethered alkynes constitute one of the most powerful and broadly applicable strategies for the step‐economical construction of cyclic alkenes. However, these reactions overwhelmingly furnish exocyclic products because the catalytic cycle typically terminates upon kinetically favored ring closure, even though the corresponding endocyclic alkenes are thermodynamically more stable. Herein, we report a catalytic enantioselective arylative cyclization of 1,n‐enynes that directly delivers thermodynamically favored endocyclic alkenes bearing an exocyclic stereogenic carbon center in high yields with excellent chemo‐ and enantioselectivities. Deuterium‐labeling experiments and control studies support a pathway in which the catalytic sequence, rather than terminating after the initial arylative ring closure, continues through a formally circuitous relay of sequential 1,2‐, 1,3‐, and 1,4‐rhodium migrations. This migration relay ultimately transposes the C═C bond to the thermodynamically favored endocyclic position, stereospecifically transfers chirality to the exocyclic stereogenic carbon center, and returns rhodium to its initial carbon attachment site. This work not only establishes a distinct mode of catalytic cyclization but also elucidates the previously unknown mechanism underlying this unusual reactivity.

title: d5‐Probed Interlocked Charge‐Structural Disorder Enables Deep Mn3+/Mn2+ Redox Chemistry in Layered Oxide Cathodes
content:
An interlocked charge‐structural disorder strategy in P2‐derived Na0.67Fe0.1Mn0.9O2 couples half‐filled d5 Fe3+ ‐mediated electronic modulation with quenched structural disorder to disrupt Mn4+/Mn3+ charge ordering and cooperative Jahn–Teller correlations. The resulting flattened electrostatic‐potential landscape and elevated Mn3+ ground‐state energy lower ion‐migration barriers and enhance Mn3+/Mn2+ reduction, enabling deeper Mn redox with reduced polarization and voltage decay.








ABSTRACT
Mn‐based layered oxide cathodes are attractive for next‐generation rechargeable batteries, owing to their abundant resources and rich redox chemistry, but achieving reversible deep Mn3+/Mn2+ redox remains challenging. Herein, we developed an interlocked charge‐structural disorder protocol in P2‐derived Na0.67Fe0.1Mn0.9O2 to regulate Mn redox and stabilize discharge voltage. A disordered cation framework is engineered through electronic configuration and atomic rearrangement, where Fe3+ (d5, half‐filled) breaks charge periodicity, and rapid quenching prevents structural reordering to eliminate Fe/Mn order. Electron energy‐loss spectroscopy (EELS) reveals suppressed Mn4+/Mn3+ charge ordering, which enables extended Mn3+/Mn2+ redox as confirmed by soft x‐ray absorption spectroscopy (sXAS). The optimized cathode quenched at 700°C nearly doubles the Mn3+/Mn2+ redox contribution within the Mg‐compatible window (1.8–1.6 V vs. Mg2+/Mg) from 15.2% to 29.4%, and it delivers 291.3 Wh kg−1 energy density (based on the mass of active cathode) with capacity retention increased from 62.4% to 87.5% over 50 cycles. Mechanistically, the interlocked disorder lowers the migration barrier by flattening the electrostatic‐potential landscape and enhances the thermodynamic driving force for Mn3+/Mn2+ by destabilizing Jahn–Teller correlations. This work establishes charge‐state disorder as a versatile design principle for layered oxide cathodes, enabling deep, reversible transition‐metal redox for advanced energy storage.

title: Thermodynamic–Kinetic Synergy Enables Neon/Helium Separation in an Anion‐Pillared Metal–Organic Framework
content:
Shell‐like electrostatic nanotraps within an anion‐pillared metal–organic framework integrate preferential Ne adsorption with markedly slower He transport, enabling thermodynamic–kinetic synergistic Ne/He separation. Ni(4‐DPDS)2CrO4 delivers a Ne uptake of 50.63 cm3 g−1, a kinetic selectivity of 113.58, and sequential collection of >99.999% He and >99.7% Ne through adsorption and temperature‐driven desorption.








ABSTRACT
Separating neon (Ne) from helium (He) remains challenging because both gases are chemically inert and weakly interacting, while classical size‐sieving principles predict faster transport for the smaller He atom. Here we address this challenge with the anion‐pillared metal–organic framework (MOF) Ni(4‐DPDS)2CrO4, whose confined pores combine narrow apertures with electrostatically heterogeneous cavities. This environment provides multiple weak contacts that favor Ne adsorption while producing an inverse diffusional response relative to the expected size trend. At 77 K and 100 kPa, the framework adsorbs 50.63 cm3 g−1 of Ne but only 0.40 cm3 g−1 of He in static adsorption, with a kinetic Ne/He selectivity of 113.58. Fixed‐bed experiments afford He with a purity above 99.999%, followed by temperature‐driven recovery of Ne with a purity above 99.7%. The results show that coordinating adsorption thermodynamics with molecular transport offers a route to separating weakly interacting gases beyond equilibrium affinity or classical size sieving alone.

title: Decoding Direct Regeneration of Spent LiFePO4: From Defect Evolution to Thermodynamic–Kinetic Barrier Engineering
content:
The rapid growth of lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4, LFP) batteries has made the sustainable recycling of spent cathodes increasingly important. In this study, we propose a multiscale defect framework for the direct regeneration of spent LFP that quantitatively correlates formation energy (ΔHf), migration barrier (Ea), and reorganization energy (λ) with the failure state of spent LFP.








ABSTRACT
The rapid growth of LiFePO4 (LFP) batteries has made the sustainable recycling of spent cathodes increasingly important for the battery circular economy. Direct regeneration has emerged as the most promising strategy because it preserves the pristine framework, minimizes energy consumption, and maximizes material value. However, the underlying principles governing regeneration remain elusive, as exemplified by the apparent thermodynamic‐kinetic paradox that metallic lithium has been reported to be ineffective for restoring spent LFP, whereas weaker reductants can achieve effective recovery. These observations indicate that regeneration is governed not by thermodynamic driving force alone, but by the coupled effects of electron transfer, ion diffusion, and lattice defects. In this study, we introduce a multiscale defect framework that correlates defect formation energy (ΔHf), migration barriers (Ea), and electron‐transfer reorganization energy (λ) with different degradation states of spent LFP. A hypothesis that the dominant barrier evolves with degradation was proposed, enabling failure‐dependent strategies ranging from relithiation and phase‐boundary engineering to defect‐guided upcycling. By transforming regeneration from empirical optimization into rational barrier engineering, this perspective provides a unified understanding of diverse restoration pathways. Finally, emerging challenges, including impurity management, AI‐assisted diagnostics, and closed‐loop materials design, are discussed to guide the development of sustainable battery recycling technologies.

title: A Phosphinidene‐Bridged P6 Platform for Phosphorus Framework Editing, Fragment Transfer, and Derivatization
content:
A phosphinidene‐bridged P6 scaffold serves as a versatile P6 platform for phosphorus framework editing. P4 release and phosphinidene transfer, together with N‐heterocyclic carbene (NHC)‐mediated framework reorganization, provide programmable access to phosphorus compounds spanning P1–P8. Extension to aluminum(I) chemistry enables further derivatization, furnishing diverse aluminum–phosphorus clusters and value‐added phosphorus products.








ABSTRACT
White phosphorus (P4) is an indispensable feedstock for organophosphorus synthesis, yet strategies for the controlled manipulation of P4‐derived polyphosphorus frameworks remain rare. Here, we report a phosphinidene‐mediated strategy that converts P4 into a phosphinidene‐bridged hexaphosphane, which functions as a versatile P6 platform rather than merely an isolable P4‐derived framework. This scaffold undergoes controlled P─P bond reorganization, P4 release, phosphinidene transfer, heteroelement insertion, and selective derivatization, providing access to phosphorus species spanning P1 to P8. Mechanistic studies with water, cyclic(alkyl)(amino) carbenes (CAACs), and N‐heterocyclic carbenes (NHCs) reveal dynamic phosphorus‐fragment transfer and carbene‐mediated framework reorganization through phosphinidene‐containing intermediates. Extension to aluminum(I) chemistry affords structurally diverse Al─P clusters that can be converted into value‐added phosphorus products including PH3 and PMe3. These results establish phosphinidene‐functionalized polyphosphorus frameworks as promising synthetic platforms for the controlled molecular manipulation of elemental phosphorus.

title: Vibrational Strong Coupling of Hydrogen‐Bonding Solvent Modes Modulates Proton Transfer in Wieland–Miescher Ketone Synthesis
content:
Here, we demonstrate that vibrational strong coupling of a solvent hydrogen bonding mode modulates product formation and stereoselectivity in a multistep organocatalytic reaction. Selective coupling of the solvent OH vibration enhances solvent‐mediated proton transfer in the rate‐determining step. Mode‐selective reactivity highlights the key role of directed vibrational energy flow in cavity‐controlled chemistry.








ABSTRACT
Vibrational strong coupling (VSC) is emerging as an efficient tool for influencing chemical reactions within an optical cavity. Here, we report the enhancement of ground‐state proton transfer in a multistep Robinson annulation reaction by directly coupling the cavity mode to a selective solvent vibrational mode that is absent in the reactants. Being a hydrogen‐bond‐donating solvent, methanol facilitates proton transfer via a hydrogen‐bonding network, and this proton transfer is further enhanced under VSC. An increase in the product formation upon coupling to the solvent O─H and reactant C═O stretch suggests a unique role of the cavity‐coupling of specific vibrational modes involved in the rate‐determining step (RDS) of the reaction. In this context, the intrinsic intramolecular vibrational energy redistribution (IVR) lifetime of the two modes acts as a key factor in determining the reaction outcome under VSC. Moreover, we find that VSC involving these modes also impacts stereoselectivity, leading to an increased enantiomeric excess (ee). This demonstration of enhanced yield and enantioselectivity under VSC highlights the pivotal role of solvent‐mode coupling in facilitating ground‐state proton transfer through hydrogen‐bonding networks, paving the way for mode‐selective control in complex multistep reactions.

title: Dipole‐Polarized Tri‐Pore COF Delivers Electrons to an O2‐Enriched Pore for H2O2 Photosynthesis
content:
Dipole polarization in an asymmetric tri‐pore BPDaPhF‐COF spatially couples O2 enrichment with electron delivery: one pore pre‐concentrates O2, while the localized dipole polarization field shuttles long‐lived photogenerated electrons to this O2‐rich pore. Via an *OOH‐mediated pathway, this pore‐matched coupling of O2 preconcentration and electron delivery accelerates the two‐electron ORR and enables efficient, selective H2O2 photosynthesis (6.04 mmol g−1 h−1), far surpassing single‐pore counterparts.








ABSTRACT
Although covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are ordered and tunable, the structural homogeneity of conventional COFs leaves charge delivery and O2 activation spatially and functionally uncoupled, limiting both H2O2 selectivity and yield. Here, we report a three‐component, tri‐pore COF by integrating para‐phenylenediamine into a binary fluorenone‐pyrene framework. The asymmetric tri‐pore architecture selectively channels O2 into one pore before reduction, while the built‐in dipole polarization field‌ directs electrons to the O2‐occupied pore. Femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy shows excited‐state carrier lifetime is doubled, thereby enabling exclusive electron delivery to that O2‐preconcentrated pore. Molecular dynamics simulations and in situ infrared spectroscopy further reveal favorable O2 adsorption behavior and an *OOH‐mediated pathway. The COF exhibits a photocatalytic H2O2 production rate of 6.04 mmol g−1 h−1 in pure water under O2, surpassing its two single‐pore counterparts by respective factors of 18.9 and 6.4. An 18.9‐fold increase in the reaction rate, far exceeding the 3.0‐fold enhancement in the electric field, is not another routine charge‐separation effect but a pore‐specific charge‐delivery effect: electrons are shuttled to the pore where O2 has already been adsorbed, and *OOH is formed predominantly at that O2‐enriched pore. For next‐generation COF photocatalysts, delivering O2 mass transport to the catalytic pore should be prioritized over simply enhancing the electric field.

title: Partial Solvation Promotes Chlorate Formation on Sea Salt Crystal Surfaces
content:
A small amount of water transforms seemingly inert sea salt crystals into reactive surfaces. At relative humidities far below deliquescence, partial solvation promotes chlorate formation in MgCl2‐enriched surface domains. Synchrotron‐based spectroscopy and molecular simulations reveal distinct interfacial environments characterized by strong electric fields and incomplete ionic solvation, highlighting an overlooked regime of interfacial redox chemistry.








ABSTRACT
Partial solvation creates interfacial environments that are neither dry solids nor bulk solutions, yet how this intermediate state controls chemical reactivity remains poorly understood. Here, we show that partial solvation at relative humidities far below deliquescence activates unexpected redox chemistry at ionic salt surfaces. Using surface‐sensitive X‐ray spectroscopy, we observe chlorate formation on Arctic sea‐salt crystals and an independent natural salt system following exposure to water vapor, whereas chlorate is absent under dry conditions. Chlorate formation is associated with partially solvated, MgCl2‐enriched surface domains. First‐principles molecular dynamics simulations reveal strong interfacial electric fields and undercoordinated hydroxide environments, providing physicochemical conditions compatible with charge separation and radical‐mediated oxidation. Our results identify partial solvation as a previously overlooked regime for activating chemical transformations at ionic surfaces and establish partially solvated salt surfaces as distinct reactive environments bridging solid‐state and aqueous‐phase chemistry.

title: A Programmable α‐Aminonitrile Platform for Tunable and Stimulus‐Responsive Hydrogen Cyanide (HCN) Delivery
content:
This work establishes α‐aminonitriles as a programmable platform for hydrogen cyanide (HCN) delivery through retro‐Strecker transformation. Structural tuning provides release half‐lives spanning 2.9–9165 min, while modular caging and click‐to‐release designs enable direct, esterase‐responsive, ROS‐responsive, and bioorthogonally activatable HCN donors with demonstrated cellular, neuroprotective, and anti‐inflammatory utility.








ABSTRACT
Despite increasing evidence that endogenous cyanide participates in cellular signaling, its biological functions remain poorly understood because programmable chemical control over hydrogen cyanide (HCN) delivery has been unavailable. Here we establish a general chemical framework that enables controlled HCN delivery by exploiting the retro‐Strecker reactiveity of α‐aminonitriles under physiologically compatible conditions. We uncover a predictable structure–reactivity relationship that allows HCN release kinetics to be rationally programmed over more than three orders of magnitude, with half‐lives ranging from 2.9 to 9165 min, primarily through nitrogen‐centered electronic effects with additional steric and conformational modulation. This unified framework further supports multiple modes of molecular control, enabling esterase‐responsive intracellular HCN delivery, ROS‐responsive activation that protects against ischemia–reperfusion injury in both OGD/R cells and MCAO mice, and bioorthogonally triggered HCN generation that suppresses LPS‐induced TNF‐α production in macrophages. Together, these studies establish α‐aminonitriles as an enabling platform that converts cyanide from an experimentally intractable toxic molecule into a chemically programmable signaling entity, providing a molecular foundation for systematic investigation of cyanide biology and its therapeutic potential.

title: Chemoselective Electrochemical Ring Cleavage of Naphthols Enabling Structural Diversification
content:
An electrochemically driven dearomative ring‐cleavage method is developed to transform easily accessible β‐naphthols into versatile, stereochemically defined ring‐opened products. Additionally, ring reconstructions yield a variety of carbocycles and heterocycles. This work establishes electrochemical dearomative ring cleavage as a programmable and scalable platform for molecular diversification and skeletal remodeling.








ABSTRACT
Structural modification of aromatic frameworks by breaking core C─C bonds is challenging due to their inherent stability. Herein, we introduce an electrochemical dearomative ring‐cleavage method that converts readily available β‐naphthols into synthetically versatile, stereodefined ring‐opened esters with broad functional‐group tolerance. Further ring reconstructions provided various carbocycles and heterocycles, highlighting the synthetic versatility of this strategy for the skeletal modification of aromatic frameworks. Mechanistic studies, including intermediate isolation, cyclic voltammetry, and electrode surface analysis, support a stepwise multielectron oxidation process. In this approach, controlled anodic oxidation, cathodically generated nucleophiles, and proton‐coupled electron transfer collectively govern chemo‐ and stereoretentive C─C bond cleavage.

title: Efficient Chirality Transfer Enables Amplified Circularly Polarized Luminescence in Chiral Metal Halides Hybrid Structures
content:
Adopting a structure‐directing strategy with a single chiral cation, two pairs of 1D hybrids, P/M‐PCA‐2Mn and P/M‐PCA‐Mn, were synthesized, which can be extended to other chiral ligand systems. In P/M‐PCA‐Mn, synergistic effects drive enhanced photophysical and chiroptical properties: Polyhedral distortion promotes chirality transfer, Mn2+ antiferromagnetic ordering may favor efficient emission, and magnetic transition dipole moment elevates the |glum| values.








ABSTRACT
Chiral organic‐inorganic hybrid metal halides have aroused considerable interest for chiroptical applications. However, developing effective structural design strategies and elucidating the underlying chirality transfer mechanisms remain challenging. Herein, utilizing a structure‐directing strategy, two pairs of enantiomeric hybrid manganese chlorides including one‐dimensional (1D) structures [R‐/S‐(C6H11NO2)3Mn]·[MnCl4] (denoted as P‐/M‐PCA‐2Mn) and R‐/S‐(C6H11NO2)MnCl2 (denoted as P‐/M‐PCA‐Mn) were synthesized based on the chiral ligands (R/S)‐(‐/+)‐piperidine‐3‐carboxylic acid ((R/S)‐(‐/+)‐C6H12ClNO2). This approach also demonstrates generality and can be extended to systems incorporating different ligands. Magnetic susceptibility measurements revealed that antiferromagnetic spin arrangement may contribute to the 7‐fold emission efficiency enhancement in P‐PCA‐Mn. Furthermore, the luminescent dissymmetry factor |glum| value increased from 1.3 × 10−3 in P‐PCA‐2Mn to 4.2 × 10−2 in P‐PCA‐Mn, which is associated with stronger intramolecular hydrogen‐bonding interactions, more pronounced structural distortion, and an enhanced magnetic transition dipole moment, collectively suggesting their potential contributions to the improved circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) performance. Through integration with liquid crystals, stepwise CPL amplification was achieved, elevating |glum| to the 10−1 order of magnitude, which exhibits the enantioselectivity of asymmetric photopolymerization. This work confirms the effectiveness of a structure‐directing strategy in boosting both luminescence efficiency and chirality transfer in chiral hybrid metal halides, and presents a novel and efficient platform for regulating CPL properties.

title: Sulfur Substitution of Oxygen‐Induced Multiferroic Phase Transition in Chiral Supramolecular Crystals
content:
We report the first chiral supramolecular ferroelectric–ferroelastic multiferroics designed via the O/S substitution‐induced multiferroic phase transition, which exhibit switching of the second‐harmonic generation circular dichroism (SHG‐CD) response.








ABSTRACT
Multiferroics exhibiting multiple ferroic orders have gained tremendous attention for decades owing to their intriguing properties and potential applications in future multifunctional devices. However, despite their unique advantages, such as inherent chirality—in contrast to traditional inorganic multiferroics, the design of molecular multiferroics with ferroelectricity and ferroelasticity remains a great challenge. Herein, through oxygen–sulfur (O/S) heavier congener substitution, we successfully designed the first chiral supramolecular ferroelectric–ferroelastic multiferroics [(R/S)‐1‐(2‐fluorophenyl)ethylamounium)(1‐thia‐15‐crown‐5)]BF4. We found that O/S substitution on parent chiral supramolecular compounds with no phase transition results in a 222F2‐type ferroelectric/ferroelastic multiferroic phase transition at 350 K, which can be attributed to the fact that the lower electronegativity of S than O weakens intermolecular interactions in the supramolecular system to reduce the energy barrier for molecular motions. Moreover, the O/S substitution induces remarkable chiral amplification, with the dissymmetry factor of the second‐harmonic generation circular dichroism (SHG‐CD) response one order of magnitude larger than that of the parent counterpart. Notably, such an SHG‐CD response can be switched from a high to a low state during the multiferroic phase transition. Our work opens up a new avenue for constructing multiferroic phase transitions in molecular systems and sheds light on the further exploration of chiral supramolecular multiferroics.

title: Photothermal Upcycling of Waste Polyolefins to Ethylene and Propylene Over Waste Plastic‐Derived Carbon Catalysts
content:
Polypropylene‐waste‐derived carbon nanospheres (PP‐C) enable rapid photothermal upgrading of polyethylene under focused light, achieving nearly complete conversion and ~60% olefin yield within 10 min. Characterizations and theoretical calculations identify defect‐rich sp2 carbon edges as active sites that facilitate charge separation and C–C bond activation. This waste‐to‐waste strategy offers a sustainable route for polyolefin valorization.








ABSTRACT
The efficient valorization of polyolefin wastes is challenged by the inertness of C─C bonds and the poor selectivity for olefins, which severely limits the conversion efficiency under mild conditions. Herein, a “treating waste with waste” strategy is proposed by using polypropylene waste derived carbon nanospheres (PP‐C) as the photothermal catalyst for polyethylene (PE) upgrading under focused Xenon light irradiation. Comprehensive characterizations identify that sp2‐C domains with abundant edge defects of PP‐C serve as the catalytic active sites, which enable outstanding photothermal conversion and facilitate photogenerated charge separation. Theoretical calculations reveal that zigzag edges of sp2‐structured graphene suppress the recombination of photogenerated charge carriers, thereby the localized electrons at the edge sites effectively weakens C─C bonds on the absorbed reactant and improves the photothermal catalytic efficiency. A remarkable olefin yield of ~60% with approximately 100% PE conversion is achieved within 10 min using PP‐C catalyst under sunlight condition, demonstrating great potential for practical applications. This work not only establishes a sustainable route for plastic valorization but also actively advances an innovative concept for the focused‐sunlight‐drives upgrading of polyolefins.

title: Stress‐Modulated Ionic Transport Limits Composite Cathode Kinetics in Solid‐State Batteries
content:
Chemo‐mechanical coupling can govern the reversal of reaction fronts between charge and discharge in solid‐state batteries. Cathode particle breathing alters electronic connectivity while generating stress fields that can suppress ionic transport in the solid electrolyte (SE). The resulting interplay can dynamically switch the dominant transport limitation and thereby determine the direction of reaction‐front propagation.








ABSTRACT
High‐energy all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs) require thick composite cathodes, yet these architectures exhibit heterogeneous reaction distributions that limit their performance. Here, we show that chemo‐mechanical transport switching governs the spatiotemporal lithiation behavior of such electrodes. By combining operando depth‐resolved diffraction with microstructure‐resolved and multi‐scale simulations, we link utilization gradients to the dominant transport pathway and demonstrate that the reversal of reaction fronts between charge and discharge arises from dynamically evolving transport limitations. This switching originates from the coupled reconfiguration of electronic and ionic transport networks during cycling. Particle breathing and interfacial delamination disrupt electronic percolation, whereas the contact‐mechanics model indicates that stress‐field interactions within the solid electrolyte (SE) can limit ionic transport. The model predicts that this suppression depends on the activation volume and elastic properties of the electrolyte and can exceed an order of magnitude as interparticle spacing decreases at high active‐material loadings. Our findings establish a direct link between chemo‐mechanical evolution and transport control in solid‐state cathodes, and highlight the need for SEs with low pressure sensitivity and sufficient mechanical compliance to enable high‐energy ASSB architectures.

title: Long‐Lived Fluorinated Foldamer Channels Conduct Protons Through a Plausible Confined Carbonyl–Water Relay
content:
Fluorinated aromatic amide foldamers form a sub‐2 Å helical channel, transporting protons across lipid bilayers while discriminating against Na+, K+, Cl−, and water. Single‐channel recordings reveal long‐lived conducting states, whereas molecular dynamics simulations, DFT computations, and H/D exchange experiments suggest a predominantly water‐depleted pore and a possible confined carbonyl‐water relay for proton transport.








ABSTRACT
Artificial proton channels that combine high conductivity with strict exclusion of water and competing ions remain challenging. Herein, we report a series of fluorinated aromatic amide foldamers (1‐6) that intramolecularly fold into transmembrane channels with angstrom‐scale pores. The lead compound, channel 1, features an intrinsic pore diameter of approximately 2.0 Å and mediates rapid H+ transport across lipid bilayers, with an EC50 value of 40 nM (∼6.0 x 10−7 mol% relative to lipid), a single‐channel conductance of 196.2 pS, and long‐lived open states lasting up to 170 s. Notably, 1 displays high H+ selectivity over Cl−, Na+, and K+ (selectivity ratios of 192.0, 132.6, and 41.3, respectively) with no measurable enhancement of water permeability. Combined molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, DFT calculations, and hydrogen‐deuterium exchange experiments indicate a predominantly dehydrated pore and support a novel confined hybrid proton‐relay mechanism, in which pyridone carbonyl O‐atoms cooperate with one or a few (protonated) water species, distinct from conventional water‐wire conduction. Beyond its transport function, 1 induces apoptosis and exhibits potent anticancer activity, with IC50 values of 2.7–5.4 µM against four cancer cell lines.

title: Identification of Potent Target VDAC1 for Hepatocellular Carcinoma Therapy with the Natural Chloroxanthone–Xanthone Heterodimer Molecule Inducing Ferroptosis
content:
(+)‐Penirmxanthone A directly targets VDAC1, destabilizes the VSTM2L–VDAC1–HK2 complex, and promotes VDAC1 oligomerization, resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis and ultimately suppressing hepatocellular carcinoma growth.








ABSTRACT
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a major cause of cancer‐related mortality, underscoring the need for actionable targets and effective small‐molecule therapeutics. Voltage‐dependent anion channel 1 (VDAC1), a key regulator of mitochondrial homeostasis, remains incompletely explored as a therapeutic target in HCC. From the endophytic fungus Penicillium sp. RM, we isolated two pairs of enantiomeric heterodimers (1 and 2) and their monomers (3 and 4). Penirmxanthone A (1) is the first reported chloroxanthone‐xanthone heterodimer, whereas penirmxanthone B (2) features a previously undescribed chloroxanthone‐gentisin scaffold. In vitro, (+)‐1 suppressed aggressive phenotypes of HCC cells and induced ferroptosis. Chemical proteomic, biophysical, and genetic analyses identified VDAC1 as a direct and functionally required target of (+)‐1. Mechanistically, (+)‐1 engages VDAC1 through K239 and N241, destabilizes the V‐Set and Transmembrane Domain Containing 2 Like (VSTM2L)‐VDAC1‐Hexokinase 2 (HK2) complex, promotes VDAC1 oligomerization, and impairs mitochondrial membrane potential and energy metabolism, culminating in ferroptosis. VDAC1 knockout attenuated these effects, whereas VDAC1 re‐expression restored them. In vivo, VBIT‐4 diminished (+)‐1‐induced antitumor and ferroptosis‐related effects. Collectively, these findings identify (+)‐1, to our knowledge, as the first natural product that directly targets VDAC1 to promote its oligomerization and induce ferroptosis, highlighting VDAC1 oligomerization as a potential therapeutic target in HCC.

title: Terminal Ligand Engineering of Clover‐Shaped Windows in Ligand‐Driven Local Pore‐Space‐Partitioned MOFs for Stepwise Enhancement of Propylene/Ethylene Separation
content:
A ligand‐driven strategy is proposed for the local pore space partition of MOFs, in which terminal ligands are employed to block the clover‐shaped windows and optimize the pore environment. This synergistic modulation stepwise improves the separation performance of C3H6/C2H4 mixtures.








ABSTRACT
Ethylene (C2H4) and propylene (C3H6) are core chemical feedstocks, and high‐purity products are critical for downstream polymer production. However, existing adsorbents generally suffer from poor compatibility between pores and target gas molecules. Herein, a ligand‐driven pore space partition strategy was proposed, whereby a cage‐like metal‒organic framework (JLU‐MOF113) was constructed through the self‐assembly of a benzothiadiazole‐functionalized ligand and trinuclear iron cluster. In the framework, the oriented thiadiazole rings on the ligands enable local pore space partition, forming clover‐shaped ultramicroporous windows. Taking JLU‐MOF113 as the parent framework, 1,2,4‐triazole (trz) and tetrazole (taz) were successfully introduced to replace coordinated H2O based on terminal ligand engineering. While further blocking the pore windows, the pore environment was optimized, resulting in the preparation of isostructural JLU‐MOF114/115. Through such stepwise regulation, the microenvironment of local pores in MOFs was successfully tailored, enabling a stepwise enhancement in separation selectivity for C3H6/C2H4 mixtures. Among them, JLU‐MOF115 exhibits excellent selectivity that surpasses many known MOFs and can separate 73.8 L/kg−1 of C2H4 with a purity of 99.95% from equimolar C3H6/C2H4 mixtures. This work enriches MOFs with locally partitioned pore characteristics and provides a novel design strategy for the improvement of gas separation performance in MOFs.

title: Enantioselective C(sp3)–C(sp3) Radical Coupling Through Photoinduced Electron Donor–Acceptor Activation
content:
A photoinduced enantioselective C(sp3)–C(sp3) radical coupling is reported for the synthesis of α‐fluoroalkylated secondary alcohols using dual electron donor–acceptor (EDA) activation and chiral nickel catalysis. The reaction features broad substrate scope and functional‐group tolerance, including late‐stage functionalization of complex bioactive molecules. Mechanistic studies further support the proposed asymmetric radical coupling pathway.








ABSTRACT
The enantioselective construction of C(sp3)–C(sp3) bonds via radical pathways remains a formidable challenge, particularly when two transient alkyl radicals must be selectively coupled within a chiral catalytic environment. Here we report a photoinduced enantioselective C(sp3)–C(sp3) radical coupling for the synthesis of α‐fluoroalkylated secondary alcohols, enabled by dual electron donor–acceptor (EDA) activation and chiral nickel catalysis. Central to this approach are two EDA activation events: one directly generates a primary alkyl radical from a carboxylic acid‐derived redox ester, whereas the other generates an alkoxy radical that undergoes intramolecular 1,2‐hydrogen atom transfer to form a secondary α‐oxy alkyl radical. Stereocontrolled interception of these radicals by a chiral nickel complex enables enantioselective C(sp3)–C(sp3) bond formation. The reaction exhibits broad substrate scope and functional‐group tolerance, including the late‐stage functionalization of complex bioactive molecules. Mechanistic studies further support the proposed asymmetric radical coupling pathway.

title: Sensitive, Flexible Circularly Polarized Light Detection Driven by Circular Bulk Photovoltaic Effect in Lead‐Free Double Perovskite Ferroelectrics
content:
Sensitive, flexible CPL detection is achieved by utilizing the circular bulk photovoltaic effect of a lead‐free double perovskite ferroelectric, with a high anisotropy factor of 0.63.








ABSTRACT
Circular bulk photovoltaic effect (CBPV) of ferroelectric materials can be utilized as a distinctive methodology to detect circularly polarized light (CPL), especially in the system of organic–inorganic hybrid perovskite ferroelectrics. However, currently reported CBPV predominantly focuses on lead‐containing hybrid perovskite ferroelectrics and the resultant CPL detectors are generally based on bulk crystals, hindering further applications of those materials. Here, sensitive, flexible CPL detection is successfully realized by using lead‐free double perovskite ferroelectrics, (C6H5CH2NH3)2CsAgBiBr7 (BCAB). Along with the spontaneous polarization, BCAB presents intriguing CBPV, which drives photovoltaic current highly dependent on the helicity of CPL. Consequently, CPL detectors using BCAB crystals deliver robust anisotropy factor up to 0.68 and high detectivity of 8.5 × 1012 Jones at zero bias. More notably, BCAB single‐crystalline thin films can be obtained by mechanical exfoliation from its bulk crystals, allowing for flexible self‐powered CPL detection with a high anisotropy factor of 0.63 at specific bending angle. The value of 0.63 reaches the highest value among the reported flexible perovskite CPL detectors. As a proof‐of‐concept, our work offers a novel path to realize sensitive, flexible CPL detection and would be helpful to design lead‐free hybrid perovskite ferroelectrics for other advanced chiroptical devices.

title: A Novel Metal‐Hydrogen‐Bonded Organic Framework (M‐HOF) Cathode Material for High‐Performance Lithium–Sulfur Batteries
content:
A novel metal‐hydrogen‐bonded organic framework (M‐HOF) can concurrently reinforce polysulfide trapping, accelerate Li+conduction, and catalyze sulfur redox by synergistic regulation of Cu–N coordination and hydrogen‐bonding network. The assembled lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries can stably operate 500 cycles at 2 C and 200 cycles at −20°C at 0.5 C respectively, exhibiting superior long‐term cycling performance at low temperature.








ABSTRACT
Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries (LSBs) are highly promising for next‐generation energy storage devices, yet their practical application is hindered by severe polysulfide shuttling and sluggish sulfur conversion kinetics. Herein, a novel metal‐containing hydrogen‐bonded organic framework (HOF‐21) is constructed and integrated with carbon nanotubes and sulfur as cathode for Li–S batteries. The synergistic combination of hydrogen‐bonding networks and Cu coordination sites enables strong polysulfide anchoring and accelerates sulfur redox conversion. Experimental characterizations and theoretical calculations reveal that the unique framework structure containing metals and rich abundant hydrogen bonds effectively immobilizes soluble lithium polysulfides, while Cu active centers induce interfacial electronic coupling and optimize the thermodynamic conversion pathway of sulfur species. Benefiting from the adsorption–catalysis synergistic regulation, the HOF‐21/CNT@S cathode exhibits enhanced reaction kinetics, suppressed polysulfide migration, and improved interfacial stability. As a result, the assembled HOF‐21/CNT@S battery delivers excellent long‐term cycling stability with a capacity decay rate of only 0.06% per cycle over 500 cycles at 2 C at room temperature. Moreover, it maintains outstanding low‐temperature adaptability, achieving 76.8% capacity retention after 200 cycles at −10°C and 90.6% retention after 200 cycles at −20°C. This work provides a promising strategy for designing advanced cathode materials toward high‐energy‐density Li–S batteries.

title: Dynamic Oxygen Spillover–Structure Feedback in Asymmetric Site Catalysts: Stability Regimes and Design Principles
content:
Dynamic oxygen spillover in asymmetric multi‐site catalysts offers a powerful route to couple catalytic activity with structural stability by directing *O, *OH, and *OOH intermediates between donor and acceptor domains. Challenges remain in tracking ultrafast migration, establishing quantitative stability boundaries, and scaling uniform multi‐atom architectures. Advances in operando characterization, multiscale simulation, and machine learning are enabling self‐healing interfaces and dynamically self‐tuning catalysts for durable energy conversion and sustainable chemical synthesis. 








ABSTRACT
Oxygen spillover refers to the transfer of oxygen‐containing species, including adsorbed intermediates and lattice‐derived oxygen, from a donor site/domain to a functionally nonequivalent acceptor through interfacial or connected surface pathways. Despite extensive studies of surface‐confined spillover, its atomic‐scale dynamics in asymmetric multi‐site catalysts remain elusive. This minireview summarizes forward, reverse, and cross‐site oxygen spillover and the key factors regulating these processes. These factors are categorized into intrinsic material properties, including composition, coordination and interfacial structures, and extrinsic operating conditions, such as applied potentials and local electrolyte environments. Moreover, we elaborate on how integrating in situ/operando spectroscopy with theoretical calculations elucidates the structure–activity relationships and dynamic structural evolution at elevated current densities. In particular, drawing on these mechanistic insights, we discuss rational design strategies for asymmetric multi‐atom site catalysts. Specifically, we emphasize how interface engineering, defect control, and self‐optimization methods promote the synergy of spillover effect and structural stability. Finally, we outline the future research direction and emphasize the urgent need to achieve higher space–time resolution in situ characterization and scalable synthesis of uniform asymmetric site catalysts for practical applications.

title: Mechanism of Zwitterionic Photochromism in Aza‐Diarylethenes Revealed by Direct Observation of a Closed‐Ring Intermediate
content:
The mechanism of zwitterionic photochromism in aza‐diarylethenes is elucidated through ultrafast transient absorption and time‐resolved infrared spectroscopy. Direct observation of a conventional closed‐ring intermediate reveals that photoinduced ring closure is followed by ground‐state rearrangement to form the zwitterionic closed‐ring isomer.








ABSTRACT
Aza‐diarylethenes represent a unique class of photochromic molecules with reaction pathways inaccessible to conventional diarylethenes. Some aza‐diarylethenes form zwitterionic closed‐ring photoproducts, but direct experimental evidence for the elementary processes remains lacking. Here, we investigate the photochromic mechanism of a benzofuran‐fused aza‐diarylethene (BF‐ADE) using steady‐state spectroscopy, transient absorption spectroscopy, time‐resolved infrared spectroscopy, oxygen‐quenching experiments, single‐crystal X‐ray diffraction, and density functional theory calculations. These complementary studies demonstrate that photoirradiation ultimately affords the zwitterionic closed‐ring isomer BF‐ADE(c‐Z), whereas thermal bleaching proceeds via the neutral closed‐ring isomer BF‐ADE(c). Femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy revealed a 1.6 ps process, and time‐resolved infrared spectroscopy provided direct evidence for the formation of the conventional closed‐ring intermediate BF‐ADE(c) within the first few picoseconds after photoexcitation. Oxygen‐quenching experiments and DFT calculations further showed that BF‐ADE(c‐Z) is generated predominantly from BF‐ADE(c) on the ground‐state potential energy surface rather than through a triplet‐mediated pathway. These results provide the first experimental validation of the proposed mechanism of zwitterionic photochromism in aza‐diarylethenes.

title: Frontispiece: Active‐Site Photothermal Energy Utilization in PET Depolymerization
content: Photothermal catalysis depends not only on heat generation, but also on the efficiency of energy delivery to active sites of the catalyst (Pd). In the Research Article e2844693, Yiming Bu, Jingliang Li, and co‐workers reveal the critical role of the local thermal environment at active sites in PET depolymerization. These findings highlight effective active‐site temperature, rather than bulk temperature, as a key factor for photothermal catalysis.

title: Outside Back Cover: Polypyridyl Coordination Motifs as Precursors for Ordered Carbonaceous Frameworks Toward High‐Density Ru Single‐Atom Catalysts (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 48/2026)
content: A new molecular landscape for single‐atom catalysis. The cover illustrates how direct carbonization of terpyridine‐based precursors yields ordered carbonaceous frameworks hosting high‐density Ru single atoms that remain stable during selective CO2 hydrogenation to formic acid. By combining structural order, microporosity, and robust metal coordination, the molecular design of the precursors opens new avenues for single‐atom heterogeneous catalysis. More in the Research Article e6197340, Takeharu Yoshii, Yasutaka Kuwahara, Tomoki Ogoshi, and co‐workers.

title: Inside Front Cover: All‐Sequence‐Defined Bottlebrush Polymers via the Passerini Iterative Exponential Growth (P‐IEG) (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 48/2026)
content: A musical score is transcribed into the chemical structure of a bottlebrush polymer. In the Research Article e8297442, Kyoung Taek Kim and co‐workers report the synthesis of all‐sequence‐defined bottlebrush polymers via Passerini iterative exponential growth (P‐IEG). This approach enables precise control over the chemistry, number, and sequence of all monomers.

title: Outside Front Cover: Preserving Proton Resolution Under Cryogenic Dynamic Nuclear Polarization for Biomolecular Solid‐State NMR (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 48/2026)
content: Dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) combined with fast magic‐angle spinning brings high sensitivity and resolution to proton‐detected NMR of biomolecular solids under cryogenic conditions. The cover illustrates this approach using HET‐s amyloid fibrils, with microwave‐driven polarization enhancement illuminating selectively labelled methyl groups and enabling resolved 1H‐13C correlations and atomic‐scale structural information. title: Unstabilized Alkyl Radicals in Photochemistry: From Emerging Precursors to Reactivity
content:
Radicals are widely recognized as key intermediates in synthetic planning and photochemistry is emerging as the method of choice for their generation. Among carbon centered radicals, unstabilized alkyl radicals are the most challenging to generate. This minireview highlights recent developments in the photoinduced or photocatalytic release of such radicals starting from purposely designed precursors.








ABSTRACT
Carbon‐centered radicals have progressively become indispensable tools in modern synthetic chemistry. Visible‐light photochemistry has emerged as a powerful platform for organic transformations, enabling the selective generation of radical species under remarkably mild and sustainable conditions. The controlled generation of unstabilized alkyl radicals, however, remains one of the most challenging and rapidly evolving frontiers in the field. In recent years, substantial efforts have been devoted to the development of novel radical precursors specifically designed to enable the efficient formation of these highly valuable intermediates under photoinduced conditions. This Minireview highlights recent advances in the design of unstabilized carbon‐centered radical precursors, systematically categorizing them according to their structural features. Particular attention is devoted to understanding how precursor design influences redox properties, bond fragmentation pathways, and so forth with the aim of laying the groundwork for the future design of increasingly efficient radical precursors and the discovery of new photochemical reactivity paradigms.

title: High Entropy Regulation of Electrostatic Repulsion and Structural Design in Layered Oxide Cathodes for Sodium‐Ion Batteries
content:
This review elucidates how entropy strategies regulate electrostatic repulsion and structural evolution in layered sodium transition‐metal oxide cathodes. It integrates sodium stoichiometry, elemental selection, configurational entropy, and phase design with O–O interactions, Na+/vacancy ordering, and slab gliding, establishing practical guidelines for the design of high‐performance electrode materials for sodium‐ion battery applications.








ABSTRACT
High entropy strategies have emerged as a promising approach for tailoring the structure and electrochemical performance of layered cathodes for sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs). Although previous studies have mainly attributed these improvements to entropy‐driven structural stabilization, the mechanisms governing phase formation and evolution remain poorly understood. Herein, we propose that electrostatic regulation, particularly the modulation of Na–Na and O–O repulsive interactions, provides an important mechanistic link between high entropy design and structural evolution. Compositional complexity reconstructs the TM–O bonding network, redistributes the charge compensation, alleviates local lattice distortion, and modulates interlayer interactions, thereby influencing the formation and evolution of P2‐ and O3‐type structures during Na+ (de)intercalation. Based primarily on configurational entropy and elemental distribution, high entropy strategies can be divided into three operational categories: high entropy doping, entropy tuning, and high entropy structure. Their phase‐dependent effects are then analyzed within P2, O3, and P2/O3 structural frameworks to clarify how entropy‐related strategies address distinct electrostatic instabilities. The correlations among sodium content, entropy level, phase structure, and electrochemical behavior are further summarized to establish practical design principles for layered oxide cathodes.

title: Near Infrared Photoswitching by Direct Excitation—A Next Frontier
content:
Molecular photoswitches finally enter the spectral realm of near‐infrared for their direct excitation. This minireview summarizes the current state‐of‐the‐art, the design principles for achieving such low‐energy light responsiveness, and the unique applications that are unlocked by it. A look to the future reveals the exciting perspectives of this emerging field.








ABSTRACT
The field of molecular photoswitches has grown tremendously over the past decades and pervaded every applied field from chemistry, biology, physics, to materials science and beyond. A main driver for continuous progress is tailoring absorption properties as a fundamental tool for controlling the light response. So far, the shift of absorption from UV light addressability into lower‐energy visible and red spectral regions has unlocked numerous unique opportunities, both in capability increase as well as in applicability of photoswitches. A next frontier has been opened more recently by extreme redshifting of absorption, allowing to enter the near‐infrared (NIR) spectral realm via direct excitation. This minireview highlights these important developments, delineates design principles to achieve NIR responsiveness in molecular photoswitches, and showcases the specific benefits that come with such low‐energy light control over molecular states. The outlook glimpses into the future and points out the particular opportunities and challenges ahead.

title: Active Electrochemical Regulation Strategies Based on Dynamic Response Mechanisms for Secondary Batteries
content:
Electrochemical regulation strategies are integrated with fundamental electrochemical theory and advanced engineering signal control, representing a promising frontier in battery regulation. This review constructs a clear theory and application framework for electrochemical regulation strategies, emphasizing the importance of active and dynamic regulation, which is expected to promote the theory‐guided optimization of secondary batteries. 








ABSTRACT
Developing advanced secondary batteries to adapt to the increasingly stringent performance requirements demands a fundamental rethinking of battery regulation strategies. Active electrochemical regulation strategies for secondary batteries are an innovative shift from static material design to dynamic electrochemical control, representing a promising frontier of battery regulation. Herein, for the first time, we provide a comprehensive review of recent advances in electrochemical regulation strategies for secondary batteries. Beginning with the fundamental electrochemical principles, this review summarizes the forefront applications of electrochemical regulation strategies, including interface optimization, electrode modulation, and electrochemical preheating techniques. The systematic mechanism analysis is conducted, emphasizing how electric field variation within batteries regulates the thermodynamic and kinetic behaviors of the constituent components, thereby determining the dynamic response of the entire system. Finally, this work outlines the existing challenges in electrochemical regulation and suggests promising directions for future research. Combined with active electrochemical regulation, it is expected to uncover foundational electrochemistry principles of battery performance enhancement, paving the way for theory‐guided optimization of secondary batteries.

title: Deciphering Anionic Chemistry in Aqueous Zinc‐Based Batteries: From Spectators to Regulators
content:
This review summarizes the key roles of anions in aqueous zinc‐based batteries, including their intrinsic physicochemical properties, coordination and solvation behavior, regulation of Zn anode reactions and cathode kinetics, and function as charge carriers. The relationships between anion properties and electrochemical behavior are highlighted, together with future directions for rational anion design. 








ABSTRACT
Aqueous zinc‐based batteries (AZBs) have emerged as promising candidates for grid‐scale energy storage systems due to the high volumetric capacity, intrinsic non‐flammability, and cost‐effectiveness. However, their practical application is limited by insufficient reversibility and sluggish reaction kinetics. In this regard, anionic chemistry plays a key role in regulating the thermodynamics and kinetics of electrode reactions. Nevertheless, most discussions in the chemistry of AZBs focus on Zn2+ behavior, and a comprehensive review of anionic chemistry is still lacking. In this review, we systematically summarize the key descriptors of commonly used anions, which affect the competitive coordination among anions, Zn2+, and H2O. We then critically analyze the effect of anionic chemistry on zinc anode reactions, including the hydrogen evolution reaction and Zn‐deposition process, elucidating structure–performance correlations between anionic properties and electrochemical behavior. Furthermore, we discuss the role of anions as charge carriers and their impact on the kinetics of cathode reactions. Finally, we conclude with a concise perspective of future research directions in anion design and mechanistic investigation. This review may provide guidance for the rational design of high‐performance AZBs for practical applications.

title: Organocatalytic Dynamic Kinetic Resolution for the Stereoconvergent Synthesis of N–N Axially Chiral Compounds
content:
An organocatalytic dynamic kinetic resolution merges reversible Pudovik addition with stereoselective phospha‐Brook rearrangement, converting racemic diastereomers into N–N axially chiral compounds. Bioinspired peptide‐phosphonium salt catalysis enables catalyst‐accelerated racemization and epimerization, affording good yields and high enantioselectivities. Mechanistic studies identify the rearrangement as stereodetermining and reveal synergistic hydrogen‐bonding/ion‐pairing control over asymmetric induction, establishing a new paradigm for axially chiral molecule synthesis.








ABSTRACT
Dynamic kinetic resolution (DKR) serves as a fundamental approach in asymmetric synthesis which enables the efficient conversion of racemic starting materials into a single stereoisomer, yet its extension to racemic diastereomers remains a formidable challenge, and reported DKR processes have largely been restricted to substrates bearing a single stereogenic element. Herein, we report an organocatalytic DKR with catalyst‐accelerated racemization and epimerization for the asymmetric construction of significant N–N axially chiral compounds through the merger of a reversible Pudovik addition with an irreversible, stereoselective phospha‐Brook rearrangement. Under bioinspired peptide‐phosphonium salt catalysis, a wide range of N–N axially chiral products were obtained in good yields and high enantioselectivities. Scale‐up synthesis and product derivatization further underscore the synthetic utility of this protocol. Mechanistic studies support a DKR process involving reversible racemization and epimerization through prochiral intermediates, identify the phospha‐Brook rearrangement as the stereodetermining step, and reveal key roles of hydrogen‐bonding and ion‐pairing interactions in catalyst‐controlled stereochemical induction. This work establishes a new paradigm for the catalytic asymmetric synthesis of axially chiral molecules.

title: Molecular Preorganization Unlocks Reversible Solid‐State Photoconversion in Dianthrylnaphthalene‐Based Molecular Solar Thermal Systems
content:
Three dianthrylnaphthalenes were synthesized and investigated for molecular solar thermal (MOST) energy storage. Naphthyl‐based bridging units preorganize the two anthracene moieties face‐to‐face, leading to improved photoisomerization quantum yield (QY) and unlocked bidirectional photoswitching in the solid state compared to previously reported ortho‐dianthrylbenzenes. 








ABSTRACT
Molecular solar thermal (MOST) systems capable of harnessing sunlight, storing it as chemical energy in the form of a photoisomer, and releasing it as thermal energy on demand represent a promising strategy for renewable solar energy utilization both in liquid‐based devices and the solid state. However, the implementation of MOST materials in the solid state is limited by restricted molecular motion in the condensed phase, which hampers the geometrical requirements for photoisomerization, as well as by inner filter effects which can prevent quantitative photoconversion or necessitate long irradiation times. To address these challenges, three dianthrylnaphthalenes were designed to pre‐organize two anthracene moieties in a face‐to‐face geometry favorable for intramolecular photodimerization. This molecular design increased the forward photoisomerization quantum yield compared to ortho‐dianthrylbenzenes, reaching 32%, while enabling solid‐state switching. In particular, the acenaphthene‐linked derivative underwent quantitative conversion to its higher‐energy photoisomer in both thin films and bulk crystalline powders. Electron diffraction analysis revealed elongated newly formed C─C bonds in the photoisomer, with refined lengths of 1.81(2) and 1.63(2) Å, exceeding the generally observed length of a Csp3─Csp3 bond. These results demonstrate how molecular preorganization can overcome limitations of anthracene‐based MOST systems and expand their potential for solid‐state solar energy storage applications.

title: Crystallography‐Dependent Plating/Stripping Kinetics and Interfacial Morphologies in Zn Metal Anodes
content:
SECCM coupled with fast‐scan cyclic voltammetry enables facet‐resolved measurements of Zn plating/stripping kinetics on single‐crystal (002), (100), and (101) surfaces. The close‐packed (002) facet exhibits the lowest exchange current density, whereas the more open (100) facet is kinetically fastest. Post‐cycling footprints preserve facet‐specific geometries, revealing crystallographically anisotropic Zn dissolution across the Zn interface.








ABSTRACT
Crystallographic orientation governs Zn deposition, dissolution, and cycling stability, but its influence on interfacial charge‐transfer kinetics remains difficult to quantify. Here, scanning electrochemical cell microscopy coupled with fast scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) is used to resolve Zn plating and stripping on single‐crystal (002), (100), and (101) surfaces. Meniscus‐confined measurements reveal facet‐dependent branch‐specific apparent zero‐current potentials and apparent exchange current densities, j0, with the kinetic ordering j0(100) > j0(101) > j0(002) for both plating and stripping. This ordering is reproduced across independently prepared electrodes and retained over different scan rates and aqueous electrolytes. Beyond charge transfer, Zn removal and regrowth are strongly crystallographically encoded: dissolution footprints preserve the symmetry of the parent facets, while potentiostatically deposited Zn adopts substrate‐dependent growth geometries. These coupled kinetic and morphological differences translate directly to battery performance. Despite its slower apparent kinetics, the close‐packed, low‐energy (002) facet exhibits the longest cycling life in Zn/Zn symmetric cells and substantially improved capacity retention in both polyaniline/Zn and Na0.33V2O5/Zn full cells, whereas the faster (100) and (101) interfaces fail earlier. These findings establish a facet‐dependent kinetics–stability trade‐off and show that durable Zn anodes require coordinated control of charge transfer, dissolution topology, and crystallographic reconstruction.

title: Bimetallic Metal‐Acetylide Frameworks for Highly Selective and Durable H2O2 Electrosynthesis
content:
A bimetallic metal‐acetylide framework (ZnTTPP‐Ni‐AF) is reported for selective electrochemical H2O2 production via 2e− oxygen reduction reaction. The catalyst achieves 94% selectivity and >90% Faradaic efficiency, with outstanding stability over 148 h. Mechanistic studies reveal that strong σ‐dominant Ni 3 dz2−${{d}_{{{z}^2}}}-$ O 2p hybridization stabilizes the *OOH intermediate and suppresses O─O bond cleavage. Synergy with Zn─N4 porphyrinic sites further lowers the *OOH formation barrier, effectively steering the reaction away from the competing 4e− pathway. 








ABSTRACT
Metal‐acetylide frameworks (MAFs) feature tunable d–π orbital hybridization between transition metal centers and π‐conjugated acetylide linkers. Here we report a two‐dimensional (2D) MAF, ZnTTPP‐Ni‐AF, assembled from zinc‐thienylporphyrin units (ZnTTPP) and nickel(II)‐bis(acetylide) linkers (─C≡C─Ni(PBu3)2─C≡C─, Bu = ─CH2CH2CH2CH3), as a selective electrocatalyst for the two‐electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e− ORR) to H2O2. In alkaline electrolyte, ZnTTPP‐Ni‐AF achieves 94% H2O2 selectivity and >90% Faradaic efficiency (FE) in an H‐cell, with excellent stability over 148 h. In a flow cell, it maintains >91% FE from 20 to 160 mA cm−2, delivering an H2O2 yield rate of 13.68 mol g−1 h−1 at 160 mA cm−2. Combined experimental and theoretical studies reveal that synergy between Zn−N4 porphyrinic centers and NiII‐bis(acetylide) motifs promotes O2 activation and stabilizes the *OOH intermediate, steering the ORR toward the 2e− pathway. Enhanced Ni‐3dz2${{d}_{{{z}^2}}}$ and O‐2p orbital hybridization facilitates proton‐coupled electron transfer to *OOH while suppressing O─O bond cleavage. This work demonstrates that engineering orbital hybridization and bimetallic cooperativity in MAFs provides an effective strategy to overcome the intrinsic activity‐selectivity trade‐off in electrocatalytic H2O2 synthesis.

title: Ultra‐Low Thermal Conductivity in Mixed Anionic CuTe2Cl: Strong Antibonding States and Lone Pair‐Induced Te Ring Puckering
content:
Strong Cu 3d‐Te 5p and Cu 3d‐Cl 3p antibonding interactions induce lattice softening, and Te 5s2 lone‐pair‐driven ring puckering enhances lattice anharmonicity, markedly suppressing heat‐carrying acoustic phonons and leading to intrinsically ultralow lattice thermal conductivity (κlat) in CuTe2Cl.








ABSTRACT
Metal chalcohalides, an emerging class of mixed‐anion compounds, have recently garnered increasing interest as they unite the exceptional stability of metal chalcogenides with the versatile electronic tunability of metal halides. Here, we synthesize single‐ and polycrystalline CuTe2Cl, a two‐dimensional layered metal chalcohalide, which exhibits intrinsically ultralow lattice thermal conductivity (κlat) of ∼0.54–0.24 W m−1K−1 between 300 and 600 K along the layered growth direction. Strong p‐d* antibonding states arising from Cu 3d‐Te 5p and Cu 3d‐Cl 3p interactions in the valence band just below the Fermi level weaken the Cu‐Te and Cu‐Cl bonds to render the lattice elastically soft. Moreover, heteroleptic polyhedral coordination enforces chemical bonding hierarchy, which, together with the stereochemically active 5s2 lone pair of Te, generates pronounced lattice anharmonicity. These effects give rise to localized low‐energy optical phonon modes, which suppress the acoustic phonons, as confirmed by phonon dispersion calculations. 5s2 lone pair driven Te‐ring puckering and lattice shearing between layers provide low‐frequency optical modes, which are experimentally identified by low‐temperature Raman spectroscopy and heat‐capacity measurements. Collectively, strong p‐d* antibonding interaction induced lattice softening and lone pair driven instability produce strong anharmonicity, which markedly suppresses the heat‐carrying acoustic phonons, leading to intrinsically ultralow κlat in mixed anionic CuTe2Cl.

title: High‐Entropy Engineering to Stabilize Single‐Atom Ru Catalysts for Efficient and Durable Water Splitting
content:
A high‐entropy‐engineered strategy to stabilize single Ru atoms on FeCoNiCrMn spinel oxides to overcome the intrinsic activity–stability trade‐off, delivering low overpotentials of 280 mV at 100 mA cm−2 for OER and 37 mV at 10 mA cm−2 for HER, a low cell voltage of 1.66 V at 1 A cm−2 for AEMWE and undamped cell performance for 1500 h.








ABSTRACT
Developing efficient and durable electrocatalysts for oxygen and hydrogen evolution reactions (OER/HER) remains fundamentally challenging due to the intrinsic trade‐off between activity and stability. We herein report a high‐entropy‐engineered strategy to stabilize single Ru atoms on FeCoNiCrMn spinel oxides to overcome the dilemma. The resulting catalyst delivers excellent bifunctional activity and stability, revealed by low overpotentials of merely 280 mV at 100 mA cm−2 for OER and 37 mV at 10 mA cm−2 for HER, a low cell voltage of 1.66 V at 1 A cm−2 for anion exchange membrane water electrolyzer and undamped cell performance at 1 A cm−2 for 1500 h. Experimental and theoretical results illustrate that single Ru atoms coordinated by O4Cl species are active centers with the lowest theoretical overpotentials for OER and HER. Uniquely, reversible oxyhydroxides reconstructed from spinel oxides occur in the OER process. Meanwhile, Ru single atoms anchored on the oxyhydroxides has much higher dissolution potential than RuO2 and catalyzes OER following the stable adsorbate evolution mechanism pathway, resulting in excellent stability. This work highlights high‐entropy engineering for stabilizing and activating single‐atom catalysts, offering new insights into rational design of advanced catalysts for future sustainable energy device development.

title: Metal‐Center‐Controlled Fenton‐Like Reactivity of Biomimetic First‐Row Transition Metal Complexes in Aqueous Anticancer Catalysis
content:
We report a water‐soluble biomimetic nonheme iron complex that selectively activates hydrogen peroxide to generate hydroxyl radicals under physiologically relevant conditions. The complex induces oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, apoptosis, and ferroptosis in gastric cancer cells, while sparing normal fibroblasts, and synergizes with paclitaxel to suppress tumor dissemination in vivo.








ABSTRACT
Catalytic oxidative cancer therapy exploits elevated hydrogen peroxide levels within tumor microenvironments to induce selective oxidative damage in malignant cells. However, many ROS‐generating therapeutic systems rely on heavy metals or structurally complex inorganic architectures, limiting their biological compatibility and catalytic selectivity. Inspired by nonheme iron‐mediated redox catalysis, we report a series of water‐soluble biomimetic first‐row transition metal complexes supported by a picolylamine‐derived nonheme ligand scaffold bearing a pendant hydroxyl group. Systematic variation of the metal center (Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn) generated divergent electrochemical behavior and distinct peroxide‐activation reactivity, yet only the iron complex, [Fe(N2Py3OH)]2+ (1‐Fe), promoted hydroxyl radical formation via Fenton‐like hydrogen peroxide activation in water. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and crystallographic analyses revealed a biomimetic coordination environment that stabilizes a quasi‐reversible Fe(II)/Fe(III) redox couple suited to catalytic peroxide activation. In gastric cancer cells, 1‐Fe induced intracellular oxidative stress, mitochondrial depolarization, lipid peroxidation, and concomitant apoptosis and ferroptosis, while exhibiting negligible toxicity toward normal fibroblasts. In combination with paclitaxel, 1‐Fe produced synergistic antiproliferative activity in vitro and suppressed peritoneal tumor dissemination in vivo without overt systemic toxicity. Collectively, these results establish biomimetic iron complexes as molecular platforms for Fenton‐like oxidative catalysis in redox‐based cancer therapy.

title: Expanding the Chemical Space of Analytes in the 2G Crystalline Sponge Method: Size‐Compensation Strategy for the Structural Analysis of Low‐Polarity Small Molecules
content:
The accessible chemical space of second‐generation crystalline sponges (2G‐CSs) is extended to low‐polarity small molecules via a modulator‐enabled strategy. The key is the size compensation between guest and modulator to achieve a snug fit within the cage cavity.








ABSTRACT
The second‐generation crystalline sponge (2G‐CS) is a novel type of crystalline sponge that incorporates hollow cages as molecular recognition modules within its crystalline framework. This advanced CS technology provides a versatile structural analysis technique applicable to a broad range of guest molecules, regardless of polarity, with molecular weights ranging from 300 to 1500. However, the method often fails when analyzing rather low‐polarity small molecules (MW 200–300) due to an “unfavorable chemical space,” where the host cavities are too large to facilitate sufficient host–guest interactions. Here we overcome this limitation by establishing a size‐compensation strategy based on cage‐mediated pair‐selective bimolecular recognition. By co‐encapsulating a target analyte with a shape‐complementary “modulator” (e.g., phenanthrene), we precisely tailor the cavity environment without the need for chemical modification of the host. This adaptive approach enabled the x‐ray structural determination of 24 of 30 low‐polarity C15 analytes, predominantly sesquiterpenoids, including absolute configuration determination for selected chiral analytes. This work translates a decades‐old molecular recognition phenomenon into a practical approach to crystallographic structure determination of low‐polarity sesquiterpenoids.

title: Smart Piezoelectric Hybrid Ceramic Membrane With the Capacity of Pulsed Responsive Self‐Cleaning and Anti‐Fouling Functions
content:
Under the pulsed pressure, the self‐powered nano‐brushes on the smart piezoelectric hybrid ceramic membrane undergo dynamic oscillation, inducing in situ self‐cleaning and effectively preventing foulant deposition on the membrane surface. In contrast, the control ceramic membrane lacking self‐powered nano‐brushes develops a dense fouling layer, leading to pore blockage and ultimately severe irreversible fouling.








ABSTRACT
Organic fouling remains a major challenge for ceramic membrane filtration because of the strong adsorption of organic foulants on membrane surfaces. Herein, a novel design strategy is proposed for smart piezoelectric hybrid ceramic membranes featuring self‐powered nano‐brushes. Specifically, a self‐powered nano‐brush smart piezoelectric hybrid ceramic membrane (ATPAA−‐PBM) with the pulsed pressure responsiveness and self‐cleaning capability was prepared by grafting negatively charged sodium PAA polymer chain (PAA−) on the surface of BaTiO3 (BTO) piezoelectric ceramic membrane. Under the pulsed pressure, alternating piezoelectric charges induced reversible conformational oscillations of the self‐powered nano‐brushes, promoting the detachment of the foulant layer by the flowing water and thereby enabling in situ self‐cleaning. Meanwhile, the grafted PAA− nano‐brushes strongly associated with water molecules to establish a 462 nm‐thick hydration layer, while generating electrostatic repulsion toward humic acid (HA), jointly preventing foulant adhesion and enabling nearly complete rejection. The membrane exhibited outstanding retention, anti‐fouling ability, and remarkable flux retention ratio (FRR = 92.3%, 10 d) during a long‐term filtration process. Consequently, a novel excellent rejection and anti‐fouling mechanism of “self‐powered nano‐brush dynamic oscillation self‐cleaning & hydration barrier” was proposed. This study provides a new perspective for the fabrication of self‐cleaning smart piezoelectric hybrid ceramic membranes.
