title: Potassium‐Concentration‐Gated C–N Coupling Enables a Volcano‐Shaped Selectivity Window for Electrocatalytic Urea Synthesis
content:
Potassium concentration opens an optimal selectivity window for urea electrosynthesis on Cu. At an intermediate K+ concentration, favorable precursor geometry alignment and balanced electronic activation minimize the *CO–*NO coupling barrier and enhance urea selectivity. Molecular simulations and infrared spectroscopy link this response to changes in reaction energetics and the interfacial environment, guiding electrolyte design for selective urea formation.








ABSTRACT
Alkali metal cations influence electrochemical interfaces, but their role in regulating urea electrosynthesis remains incompletely understood. Here, we combine constant‐potential ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), classical molecular dynamics (cMD), flow‐cell electrolysis, and in situ infrared spectroscopy to investigate how cations affect urea formation from CO2 and nitrate on Cu. Among Li+, Na+, K+, and Cs+, K+ affords the lowest calculated barrier for direct *CO–*NO coupling and the highest measured urea Faradaic efficiency. Varying the K+ concentration reveals a volcano‐shaped dependence of urea activity and selectivity, with a maximum at a partial current density of 13.62 mA cm−2 and Faradaic efficiency of 24.50% near 1.20 M K+. AIMD calculations identify a minimum coupling barrier at an intermediate nominal K+ concentration and elucidate how K+ concentration regulates precursor geometry and charge redistribution. Complementary cMD simulations reveal concentration‐dependent changes in interfacial reactant distributions and water structure, with infrared spectral features providing experimental evidence of changes in interfacial reaction chemistry. Together, these results establish an optimal K+ concentration window governed by the coupled roles of elementary‐step kinetics and electrolyte organization in urea electrosynthesis.

title: Dynamic Soft‐Confinement via Hydrogen‐Bonded Organic Frameworks Reshapes C–C Coupling Interfacial Chemistry at Bi1–Bi2 Sites
content:
A dynamic soft‐confinement catalytic strategy by in situ constructing a disordered HOF layer on Bi3O4Br surfaces has been proposed to boost C–C coupling from CO2 photoreduction.








ABSTRACT
The core bottleneck in photocatalytic CO2 reduction toward multi‐carbon oxygenates lies in the thermodynamic‐kinetic dual limitations of the C–C coupling step. Conventional strategies have focused on intrinsic electronic structure optimization of active sites while overlooking the critical influence of the reaction microenvironment on coupling probability. Herein, we propose a dynamic soft‐confinement catalytic strategy by in situ constructing a disordered hydrogen‐bonded organic framework (HOF) layer on Bi3O4Br surfaces, thereby establishing an HOF/Bi3O4Br integrated photocatalytic system. The introduction of HOF not only induces the formation of asymmetric Bi1–Bi2 coupling sites but also establishes a dynamic hydrogen‐bonding microenvironment surrounding them. This microenvironment enhances CO2 coverage near the coupling sites by constructing a persistent carbon source enrichment layer. Simultaneously, the interfacial polarization field promotes exciton dissociation and directs electron transport toward the Bi1–Bi2 sites. Furthermore, the reconfigurable hydrogen bonds impose orientational soft confinement on *CO intermediates, guiding them into spatial configurations favorable for *OCCO bond formation. This soft‐hard synergistic interfacial design enables 0.7HOF/Bi3O4Br to achieve a CH3COOH production rate of 325.12 µmol g−1 h−1 with 98.81% product selectivity under sacrificial agent‐free conditions. This work demonstrates that dynamic microenvironment programming around active sites constitutes a critical pathway for overcoming the photocatalytic C–C coupling bottleneck.

title: Lewis Acid–Base Pairs in Photo/Electrocatalysis: Cooperative Mechanisms, Design Strategies, and Applications
content:
Lewis acid–base pairs (LPs) provide synergistic dual active sites for regulating electron transfer and molecular activation. This review summarizes the mechanisms, construction, characterization and applications of LPs in photo/electrocatalytic energy conversion and environmental remediation, together with future opportunities for rational LPs design.








ABSTRACT
Developing high‐performance and robust catalysts is essential for advancing photo/electrocatalytic technologies for sustainable energy conversion and environmental remediation. Single‐component catalysts inherently suffer from linear scaling relations in electrocatalysis and the trade‐off between light‐response scope and redox abilities in photocatalysis, failing to dynamically modulate adsorption strength of multiple intermediates. To circumvent these thermodynamic limitations, the precise introduction of Lewis acid–base pairs (LPs), specifically frustrated Lewis pairs (FLPs), has emerged as a sophisticated strategy to overcome the inherent trade‐off between activity and stability. By modulating the spatial and electronic synergy between electron‐accepting (Lewis acid) and electron‐donating (Lewis base) sites, LPs enable unique small‐molecule activation mechanisms. This dual‐site cooperative synergy provides tailored adsorption strengths for diverse reaction intermediates and significantly reduces kinetic energy barriers, thereby enhancing both catalytic activity and stability. This review critically elucidates the fundamental mechanisms and design principles of LPs in photo/electrocatalysis, and systematically highlights their crucial applications in sustainable energy conversion and environmental remediation. Finally, we outline the remaining challenges, emphasizing the necessity of coupling advanced characterization with density functional theory calculations to unravel dynamic structure‐activity relationships, thereby guiding the rational design of LPs‐engineered catalytic systems for practical applications.

title: From Synapses to Security: Morphological Transformation Organic Electrochemical Transistors for Edge Intelligence
content:
A morphology‐driven dual‐mode organic electrochemical transistor is presented, which provides one‐way functional conversion from synaptic computing to hardware security through a simple solvent treatment. The morphological transformation leads to distinct synaptic and physical unclonable function.








ABSTRACT
Neuromorphic computing and hardware‐level security are both critical for next‐generation edge intelligence systems, yet integrating these functions within a single device remains challenging because synaptic operation requires uniform conductance modulation, whereas physical unclonable functions (PUFs) rely on intrinsic randomness. Here, we report a morphology‐driven dual‐mode organic electrochemical transistor (OECT) based on a P3HT:PBA:Triton X‐100 blended active layer that undergoes a one‐way functional conversion from synaptic to PUF operation through a simple acetone soaking process. In the synaptic mode, the device exhibits a ∼20‐fold higher long‐term memory (LTM) value than the P3HT‐based OECT and a paired‐pulse facilitation index of up to 180%. In addition, Pavlovian associative learning and reservoir computing were demonstrated using the experimentally measured synaptic responses. Following solvent‐induced morphological transformation, the device exhibits device‐to‐device electrical variations, exhibiting PUF metrics of ∼50% uniformity, an average inter‐HD of 50.89%, and an entropy of 0.99. These results demonstrate that morphology‐driven functional conversion enables synaptic and PUF functions to be realized within a common organic electronic platform.

title: Single‐Vesicle Functional Nanophenotyping Reveals Heterogeneous PD‐L1 Accessibility in Triple‐Negative Breast Cancer (Small Methods 22/2026)
content:
Front Cover
High‐speed atomic force microscopy reveals how anti‐PD‐L1 antibodies dynamically engage individual tumour‐derived extracellular vesicles. Single‐vesicle functional nanophenotyping uncovers striking heterogeneity in PD‐L1 accessibility, distinguishing persistent from transient antibody interactions. The cover illustrates this nanoscale landscape, where extracellular vesicles released from cancer cells encounter antibodies under the probing tip of high‐speed AFM, revealing their functional surface diversity. More in article number e71041, Richard W. Wong and co‐workers.

title: Downsize Effect on Photocatalytic Syngas Production of a 2D Metal Organic Framework—Tuning the Selectivity From HER to CO2RR via Dimensional Modulation and Mechanical Exfoliation of 2D Metal‐Organic Layers (Small Methods 22/2026)
content:
Back Cover
Tuning the selectivity from hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) to CO2 reduction is highly desirable. In article number e70843, Rajat Saha, Debmalya Ray, Hermenegildo García Gómez, Carlos J. Gómez García, and co‐workers have prepared a 2D metal–organic framework (MOF) and converted it into a 1D MOF via dehydration‐rehydration and into an exfoliated 2D MOF by liquid phase exfoliation. Photocatalytic CO2 reduction shows that the bulk 2D MOF has higher selectivity for HER while the 1D and exfoliated MOFs show CO enriched syngas production.

title: Superoxide Dismutase‐Functionalized Titanium Dioxide Colloidosomes for Enhanced UV Protection and Persistent ROS Suppression
content:
SOD‐functionalized TiO2 colloidosomes (STCs) are self‐assembled from SOD‐adsorbed TiO2 nanoparticles for enhanced UV protection and persistent ROS suppression. The hollow mesoporous shell enhances UV shielding, while interfacially immobilized SOD scavenges photogenerated superoxide in situ. STCs maintain >95% ROS inhibition over repeated UV irradiation and show low cytotoxicity in the tested HaCaT cells, offering a durable antioxidant strategy for TiO2‐based UV filters. 








ABSTRACT
Titanium dioxide (TiO2), serving as a prominent inorganic ultraviolet (UV) filter, has been widely utilized in photoprotective formulations. However, its photocatalytic activity under UV irradiation generates reactive oxygen species (ROS), thereby raising significant concerns regarding photochemical safety. Although antioxidant coatings have been proposed to suppress TiO2‐induced ROS, persistent ROS suppression remains challenging due to the intrinsically sacrificial nature of conventional antioxidant components. Herein, we report an efficient strategy for constructing superoxide dismutase (SOD)‐functionalized TiO2 colloidosomes (STCs) for persistent ROS suppression. SOD is first electrostatically adsorbed onto TiO2 nanoparticles, followed by droplet‐confined self‐assembly of the resulting SOD–TiO2 nanoparticles into hollow mesoporous colloidosomes. This hierarchical design enables in situ scavenging of photogenerated ROS at the TiO2 interface while stabilizing SOD. Compared with bare TiO2 NPs, the STCs exhibit an approximately 1.81‐fold enhancement in Sun Protection Factor (SPF). Moreover, the STCs maintain ROS inhibition efficiencies above 95% over three consecutive 6 h UV irradiation cycles and exhibit low cytotoxicity in the tested HaCaT cells. This study provides a feasible strategy for the development of TiO2‐based UV filtration materials that integrate enhanced UV protection with persistent enzymatic antioxidant functionality, highlighting their potential applications in advanced photoprotective materials and sunscreen formulations for human health.
